ARTICLE · EDUCATION · BANGLADESH

Present in class, absent from learning.

By Md. Shawon Masud

Why Bangladesh needs a teacher evaluation system.

A poster circulated by the Dhaka University Students Alliance (DUSA) recently put a number on something many students already suspected: 71 percent said they attend class only to protect the attendance percentage they need to sit exams, 26 percent said they attend and pick up something along the way, and just 2 percent said they came mainly to learn. DUSA published no methodology, but the pattern it describes is familiar across Bangladesh’s 53 public universities, not Dhaka University alone.

That is the one immediate reform I would ask the government to make: a mandatory, standardized Teacher Evaluation System across every public university in the country, built on quality-assurance infrastructure the University Grants Commission (UGC) has already funded but never enforced.

The problem is structural, not personal. Writing in this paper in March 2023, lecturer Asmat Islam noted that Bangladesh’s public universities, unlike the global norm, give students no formal channel to evaluate their teachers. The Business Standard made a similar point in 2024, calling structured evaluation something public universities have simply never adopted. A Dhaka Tribune column this July offered a vivid illustration: a Dhaka University course where the instructor held two classes across an entire semester, in a system that requires twenty to twenty-four, with no consequences, because no student had a formal channel to flag it. Ask around almost any public university, and similar stories surface within seconds.

Most private universities already run some version of teacher evaluation, because UGC’s Institutional Quality Assurance Cell framework, funded since 2009 and reinforced by the Bangladesh Accreditation Council Act of 2017, effectively requires it of them. Public universities built the same infrastructure but were never required to use it meaningfully. Dhaka University’s own quality cell flagged “teacher’s evaluation” as a goal during a 2015-2018 self-assessment; nearly a decade later, no binding, university-wide system exists there, or almost anywhere else in the public sector.

This is not an academic-only concern. Per the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ Labour Force Survey 2024, roughly 885,000 graduates were unemployed, the largest single group among the country’s jobless, at a rate nearly three times the national average and more than double what it was eight years ago. Employers describe this as a skills gap, not a shortage of degrees, one that starts in classrooms nobody is required to evaluate.

Evaluation still has to be designed carefully. Where scores are tied too tightly to pay, some teachers respond by inflating grades rather than teaching better. A sound system needs anonymous student feedback, peer classroom observation, and public records of whether syllabi were actually delivered, feeding transparently into promotion and renewal decisions, not just one popularity number.

None of this needs new legislation. It needs a UGC directive requiring every public university to finally use the quality-assurance offices it already funded them to build. Seventy-one percent of students showing up only to sign an attendance sheet is not a Dhaka University problem. It is a national one, and it deserves a national fix.
